name: Marshall Islands
summary: Twenty-nine coral atolls in the central Pacific; German, Japanese and then US-run, the US tested 67 nuclear weapons at Bikini and Enewetak (1946–58). Independent in free association with the US since 1986.

location.value: In the central Pacific north of the equator: 29 atolls and 5 islands in two chains, Ratak and Ralik, with about 180 km² of land.

terrain.value: Low coral atolls, about 2 m above sea level.

climate.value: Tropical and hot all year, with wetter southern atolls and drier northern ones; north-east trade winds blow much of the year.

resources.value: Fish, especially tuna in its huge sea zone; coconuts for copra and oil; and pandanus and breadfruit.

disasters.value: Cyclones, droughts and rising sea levels.

population.value: About 40,000 in the mid-2020s and falling as people move to the US; the 2021 census counted about 42,000.

urbanisation.value: Most people live on crowded Majuro, the capital, and on Ebeye in Kwajalein Atoll.

disease.value: Fallout from tests such as Castle Bravo (1954) caused radiation illness on Rongelap and Utrik; today diabetes is very common.

migration.value: Under the Compact, Marshallese can live and work in the US, and many have settled in Arkansas, Hawaii and Washington State.

economicBase.value: US Compact aid, fishing licences for tuna boats, copra, rent for the US base on Kwajalein, and a large international ship registry.

tradeRoutes.value: Shipping through Majuro, a busy tuna transshipment port, and air links via Majuro and Kwajalein to Hawaii and Guam.

wealth.value: A lower- or upper-middle-income economy, depending on aid and fishing licences.

moneyAndTax.value: The US dollar is the currency; government income comes mostly from Compact grants, fishing fees and import taxes.

inequality.value: Gap between the capital and outer islands.

governmentType.value: A parliamentary republic: the Nitijela (parliament) elects a president who is both head of state and head of government.

keyRulers.value: Amata Kabua, a high chief, was the first president (1979–96); foreign minister Tony deBrum (died 2017) led its climate diplomacy.

succession.value: Presidents are chosen by the Nitijela after general elections every four years and can be removed by votes of no confidence.

stability.value: Generally stable and peaceful, with regular elections and peaceful changes of government since self-rule in 1979.

eliteConflict.value: Families of iroij (high chiefs), such as the Kabua family, have long been powerful in politics and in disputes over land.

armyAndTech.value: No army: a national police and a sea patrol, with defence provided by the United States, which runs a missile test site on Kwajalein.

territoryChange.value: No change since 1986; it claims Wake Island (Enen-kio), which the United States holds.

alliancesRivals.value: Compact of Free Association with the United States (since 1986), which gives US defence and aid. Recognises Taiwan.

inventions.value: Traditional navigation by stars and swells.

scienceEducation.value: University of the South Pacific campuses.

openness.value: Very open and import-dependent: most food and fuel are shipped in, and citizens can travel freely to the United States.

communicationTransport.value: Inter-island ships and small planes link the outer atolls to Majuro and Kwajalein, which have the main airports and ports.

religion.value: Mostly Protestant Christian, especially the United Church of Christ, brought by American missionaries from 1857; also Catholics and others.

languageWriting.value: Marshallese and English are official; Marshallese is written in a Latin alphabet devised by missionaries in the 1800s.

artsArchitecture.value: Fine weaving of pandanus mats, baskets and fans, outrigger canoes, and stick charts that map ocean swells for navigation.

sharedIdentity.value: A strong Marshallese identity based on clan land, the language, canoe traditions and shared memory of the nuclear tests.

dailyLife.value: Families share small houses; food includes breadfruit, pandanus, fish and coconut, now mixed with imported rice and tinned food.

neighbours.value: The Federated States of Micronesia to the west, Kiribati and Nauru to the south, and Wake Island to the north.

ideasReligions.value: Christianity spread by missionaries, the customary authority of iroij chiefs, and campaigns for nuclear justice and climate action.

colonisation.value: German (1885), Japanese (1914), then US trust territory (1947–86).

riseSignals.value: Self-government under its own constitution from 1979; full self-rule in free association with the US when the Compact took effect in 1986.

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge; its world profile rose through climate diplomacy, as at the 2015 Paris climate talks.

declineSignals.value: Rising sea levels threaten the low atolls with flooding and salt water, and emigration to the US is shrinking the population.

outcome.value: Still in existence as an independent republic in free association with the United States.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
